findings.section: DAG intro (revertibility claim) · Phase 1 exit gate · Phase 6 deferred list
findings.message: The plan claims globally that 'each merged wave is revertible without reverting later waves via the four per-pillar off-switch flags', and Phase 6 explicitly DEFERS removing all four flags ('they stay as supported operational levers until the Butler effort decides otherwise'). But a functional static-vs-embedded flag requires the embedded blob to still exist — and C1's Phase-1 exit gate requires the blob GONE (net ≥7,000-line shrink measured at the phase-end commit, 'no embedded frontend blob larger than ~50 lines'). You cannot simultaneously delete 7,300 lines from anchor_gui.py and keep a runtime lever that re-serves them. As written, a future maintainer reading the hybrid-state matrix will find a named, 'supported' configuration (embedded frontend) that has no code behind it — or worse, the team will keep the blob alive in some retrievable form to honor the matrix, silently failing C1. Pick one: the flag dies at Phase-1 exit (revert = git revert, stated honestly, and the DAG's revertibility claim is corrected to three flags), or the C1 bar is amended. The plan currently asserts both.

The total order is 'sort by (ts, writer_id, writer_seq)'. Because ts is the PRIMARY key, a backward wall-clock step (NTP correction, DST-adjacent skew) reorders a SINGLE writer's own events against its own monotonic writer_seq — the exact property writer_seq exists to guarantee. Cross-writer it is worse: the dashboard's job_launch_requested and the supervisor's job_launched are causally ordered but their wall clocks are independent; a few-ms inversion puts the result before the intent in every derivation, parity run, and rebuild_index replay. The envelope carries correlation_id and causation_id, yet the merge ignores both. Deterministic ≠ correct: the parity gate will re-derive views in a causally wrong order and either flag phantom divergence or, worse, converge on a wrong-but-stable derivation a future maintainer cannot debug. Fix: within a writer, writer_seq must dominate (merge segments as already-ordered streams, k-way merged by ts only ACROSS writers), and cross-writer causal pairs need causation_id-aware ordering or an explicit tolerance rule in the parity gate.

findings.section: Journal writer model / Phase 3 two-tier parity gate / Phase 5 emitter handover
findings.message: Post-split, the dashboard emits job_launch_requested, then IPCs the supervisor, which emits job_launched. If the IPC hop or the launch itself fails, the intent event is journaled but no legacy job record ever exists — a journal-ahead event that ages past the tail window and is then, by the plan's own rule, 'classified BUG'. Every legitimately failed launch attempt therefore becomes a permanent parity-gate BUG. The ownership table's job family (launched/finished/cancelled/gate_asked/gate_answered) contains no job_launch_failed or intent-expired compensating event, and the parity rules have no notion of an intent whose correlation chain legitimately terminated without a store write. A gate that cries BUG on a normal failure path trains the future maintainer to ignore BUG — killing the one signal C3 exists to provide. The plan needs either a compensating failure event owned per the table, or an explicit parity rule for intent-kind events with terminated correlation chains.

findings.section: Journal writer model — emitter-ownership table / failure mode (b)
findings.message: The invariant is 'exactly ONE owning writer per event type, checked in' — but mode:'inline' makes ownership follow the JOB HANDLE, which is per-job, not per-type. During a supervisor flap (dashboard's IPC times out and falls back inline while the supervisor is actually alive, or the supervisor recovers mid-degradation), job_finished events for different jobs legitimately appear in BOTH segments in the same window — and a false-degradation race can produce the same job launched twice (once inline, once supervised) under one correlation_id. The tripwire, parity gate, and payload-completeness gate 'all read the same table', but a static per-type table cannot adjudicate which writer was legitimate for which event at which instant. As specified, the gates either accept any writer for the job family (the invariant is unenforceable theater) or flag legitimate inline emissions as violations. The table needs a per-event legitimacy rule (e.g., ownership resolved by which process's job dir holds the handle record, checkable at verification time) and the degraded-mode transition needs a walked scenario like the C4 one — it is currently the least-specified failure mode in a section that prides itself on enumerating six.

findings.section: Phase 4 — cookie verdict application / ops-cutover gate
findings.message: C2 requires 'browser page navigation still working (cookie or equivalent)'. The plan spikes cookie-THROUGH-WS survival and applies the verdict in Phase 4, and the ops-cutover gate mints a token into NSSM env — but nowhere does any phase specify how John's browser ACQUIRES the cookie in the first place: no login/handshake route, no Set-Cookie flow, no OPEN_ROUTES entry for a bootstrap path, no statement of cookie attributes (HttpOnly, SameSite, lifetime) or re-establishment after expiry on the iPad PWA over Tailscale. The day the tokenless-401 live assert passes, GET / itself is gated — with what, exactly, in the browser? A future maintainer (or John at 7am) hits a 401 on the home page with no documented way in. This is the single most user-visible seam in the whole auth pillar and it is the one left implicit. The cookie-establishment flow must be a named Phase-4 deliverable with its own OPEN_ROUTES-reviewed entry.

findings.section: Phase 1 — shrink measurement / census margin arithmetic
findings.message: 'The NET wc -l delta on anchor_gui.py … with ALL new seam code counted against it wherever it lives' is self-contradictory: a single-file wc -l delta on anchor_gui.py mechanically CANNOT count seam code that lives in other files (bootstrap builder module, static-route wiring elsewhere). The census arithmetic (gross − ≤400 seam) reveals the intent, but the formal gate definition a Foreman wave will actually execute is ambiguous — is the number delta(anchor_gui.py), or delta(anchor_gui.py) minus new lines added in named seam files? Two readings differ by up to the whole seam budget, i.e., potentially the entire stated margin. State the formula explicitly: net = (pre-tag wc − phase-end wc on anchor_gui.py) − Σ(new lines in an enumerated seam-file list).

findings.section: Journal writer model — cli segment lock / Phase 3 journal.py
findings.message: journal.py takes an msvcrt.locking per-append lock on the cli segment. msvcrt is Windows-only; the repo's binding constraint (enforced by distro.py's import scan philosophy) is 'must run on any machine with Python 3.8+', with ONLY pywinpty exempted and ONLY behind a lazy terminal-only import. journal.py is core shared code imported by the dashboard, the supervisor, and anchor.py — an unconditional msvcrt import breaks every non-Windows consumer of anchor.py, and even a lazy import leaves the CLI-writer path undefined off-Windows. Name the portable strategy (fcntl/msvcrt shim, or O_APPEND single-write-per-line semantics which are atomic enough for short lines on both platforms) or declare and justify a second platform exception through the same reviewed path pywinpty got.

The writer set is closed at dashboard/supervisor/cli, yet the envelope's actor.kind already anticipates 'healthcheck-synthetic' — and anchor_healthcheck.py is a FOURTH OS process that boots an in-process server and exercises mutating endpoints. Its v2–v5 walks use temp ANCHOR_DATA_DIRs (journals go to temp — fine), but the plan never PROVES that every healthcheck mutation is temp-scoped once the tripwire's ENFORCE mode and the journal instrumentation are live; any journaled mutation it performs against the real data dir would append to the 'dashboard' segment from a second process, violating single-writer-per-file — the model's foundational invariant — silently. Either give the healthcheck process its own writer_id/segment, or add an explicit gate asserting the healthcheck emits zero events into the live journal directory. The reviser caught the CLI's third-writer hole; this is the same hole one process over.

The claim 'the C3 completeness guarantee survives the split with zero exceptions' rests entirely on the inline seam and the stub-seam matrix — both exercise the IN-PROCESS emit path. The two live probes (spawn claude.exe --version; restart supervisor with sacrificial child) assert credentials and job-object breakaway but never assert that the REAL supervisor service, under its NSSM account with its AppEnvironmentExtra-cloned env, actually wrote job events to its own segment with correct writer_seq recovery. Env drift (ANCHOR_DATA_DIR missing from the cloned env, path resolution under the service account) is exactly the failure class inline tests cannot see. Add one line to probe (a) or the C4 runbook: after the live job, assert its lifecycle events are present in the supervisor segment on disk. Cheap, and it closes the only untested writer.

Phase 0 is sized M (2–3 Foreman waves) yet enumerates ~13 deliverables including a census SCRIPT, five scripted Playwright stateful flows (terminal-open-and-type via stub PTY is not an afternoon), a full consumer inventory across launchers/scheduled tasks/personal scripts, the tripwire wrapper run across suite+healthcheck, a shipped-and-live-deployed contract shim touching both renderers plus _postJson plus a server-side 409 path, a shipped drain script, sentinel anchors + a freshness gate, TWO time-boxed spikes with real-client testing (iPhone PWA over Tailscale), healthcheck_repeat.py, and three process codifications. That is 4–5 waves of work labeled as 2–3. A future maintainer inheriting the plan mid-effort reads the sizing as commitments; an undersized foundation phase is how 'never-broken increments' gets rushed. Re-size honestly or explicitly move the Playwright flows and healthcheck_repeat.py into the trailing-allowed set alongside the spikes.

findings.section: Phase 4 — warn-mode soak / zero-arms exit gate
findings.message: Each route batch requires: deploy warn → soak A DAY on the live service → review warn log as a gate artifact → deploy enforce, and auth flips may never share a deploy with the JS that calls them. With ~125 arms in 'small reviewed batches', that is weeks of serialized wall clock — none of which is captured by 'L (3–4 waves)', and all of which now sits behind a BLOCKING exit gate (zero arms). The predictable failure mode is batch inflation near phase end to close the gate — exactly the rushed migration the soak discipline exists to prevent. State the batch size and expected batch count, or explicitly allow warn-soaks for multiple batches to overlap, so the exit gate's cost is sized rather than discovered.

Phase 2 preserves the old data dir 'read-only for a week'; Phase 6 — several L phases later — 'concludes the old data dir's read-only week'. Those are months apart. Either the retention is actually until-Phase-6 (say so) or the week concludes inside Phase 2/3 and Phase 6's line is dead text.

Phase 0 injects the ANCHOR_BUILD script tag into BOTH renderers and X-Anchor-Build into _postJson; Phase 1 then calls increment 1 a 'pure verbatim move, census-confirmed zero interpolations' and separately 'absorbs' the build id into ANCHOR_BOOT. The moved blob is post-shim, and the absorption is a real edit during the move — so the pinned-fixture diff will carry shim deltas that must appear on the enumerated-delta token list. Not a design flaw, but the 'pure verbatim / zero interpolations' language will be false by a few lines the moment Phase 0 ships; pre-list the shim tokens now so the first parity run doesn't open with a gate failure.

The plan moves job ownership into a separate process but never mentions the armed orphan-kill machinery that keys off in-process job state. Today's orphan discriminator (zombie_hunter.live_owner_ids) computes 'live owner' from the DASHBOARD'S view: PTY-attached set ∪ job_runner._holder_is_active ∪ parent-owned. Post-split, the dashboard no longer holds the job handles — _holder_is_active in the dashboard process will report supervisor-owned jobs as NOT active, so a supervisor-owned session with no open browser stream becomes classifiable as an orphan and the Swarm View / armed kill-daemon can freeze or kill exactly the work the split exists to protect. The repo marks this discriminator SAFETY-CRITICAL (2026-06-30). The in-memory rebuild table covers dashboard structures (_LIVE, _JOB_DIRS, lane locks) but zombie-hunter's live-owner provider is not a rebuild row and is not named anywhere in Phase 5. The C4 live demo could pass (short window, daemon not firing) while the regression ships. Phase 5 needs an explicit row: live_owner_ids' job_active provider must query the supervisor (or the merged journal) before the external seam goes live.

findings.section: Dependency DAG & sequencing rationale / Phase 4 exit gate
findings.message: The DAG edge 'Phase 5 after Phase 4' is justified by IPC reusing the route-table module + token helper — but that module exists on DAY ONE of Phase 4 (rows-first: every route gets a declared row immediately). What the plan actually gates Phase 5 behind is Phase 4's new C2-BLOCKING exit gate: migrating ~125 handler bodies to zero legacy arms across 3–4 waves. The supervisor consumes none of that handler migration. Meanwhile C4 — the restart-survival keystone the North Star calls non-negotiable, and the one pillar relieving John's real daily pain (every restart kills in-flight jobs) — lands last among pillars, behind weeks of mechanical body migration, and every per-wave smoke ritual in Phases 0–4 performs an nssm restart that kills any in-flight job. Steel-manning the plan's own 'highest-value first' re-cut logic (used to pull the journal forward), the same logic says Phase 5's jobs-half can start once the table module + warn-mode auth + the Phase-3 ownership table exist, concurrent with or immediately after the enforce flips — not after the zero-arms drive-down. The hard gate is right for C2; making it a prerequisite for C4 is an over-constrained edge the DAG should either relax or explicitly defend.

findings.section: Phase 3 — journal-first write order / two-tier parity gate
findings.message: Two commitments contradict. Journal-first-by-decree says an orphaned journal event (emit succeeded, legacy write then failed or the process crashed between them) is 'a benign intent record with an idempotent replay path.' The Tier-2 gate says journal-ahead OLDER than the tail window 'is classified BUG.' The crash-between-writes case — the exact scenario journal-first is designed to make benign — produces precisely a beyond-window journal-ahead event, so the designed-for, called-benign failure mode is permanently flagged BUG by the gate that proves C3. Either the classification needs a reconciled/acknowledged state (journal-ahead + replay-tool-converged → resolved, not BUG), or 'benign' is the wrong word and the plan should say every orphan is a defect requiring operator replay. As written, the first real crash makes the daily parity gate red forever with no defined path back to green, which corrodes the gate's authority (C7's 'suite stays green' meets a gate that can't self-heal).

findings.section: The journal writer model — seq/lock semantics
findings.message: The total order for derivation, parity, and replay is sort-by (ts, writer_id, writer_seq). Wall clocks — even on one machine — step backwards (NTP correction, resume-from-sleep on a desktop that sleeps nightly), and ts resolution ties across writers are resolved LEXICALLY, which happens to sort 'dashboard' before 'supervisor' today but is a coincidence, not a design. A causally-ordered pair (dashboard job_launch_requested → supervisor job_launched → supervisor job_finished) can merge out of order under a clock step, and rebuild_index / the replay tool — whose correctness IS criterion C3's 'provably derivable' — silently apply last-write-wins reductions in the wrong order. The envelope already carries causation_id; the merge should use it (or a hybrid logical clock: max(seen_ts+1, wall)) as a tie-and-regression breaker, and the parity gate should classify a causation edge that sorts backwards as BUG. Right now clock regression is the one failure mode NOT in the enumerated six, and it's the one that corrupts derivation rather than just losing a line.

The shim's protection premise has a hole at both ends. (1) Clients that predate the shim deploy — the already-open stale tab and the PWA-cached iPad client, the two named beneficiaries — never send X-Anchor-Build at all, and the plan doesn't say what the server does with a MISSING header. Reject it and you break anchor_healthcheck.py's endpoint walk, the CLI, and every personal script (a C7 breakage in the 'one behavior-bearing deploy'); allow it and every pre-shim client silently bypasses the shim, so the mechanism only protects tabs opened AFTER the deploy that needed protecting least. (2) The carrier rides _postJson only — WS/SSE attach and GET navigations from a stale client carry no build id, so a stale tab can hold a live terminal WebSocket across a protocol-changing deploy unchecked. The shim needs a stated missing-header policy (allow + log, with the banner delivered by a different channel for pre-shim clients, e.g. a version probe on next poll) and an honest statement of which surfaces it does NOT cover.

findings.section: Dependency DAG — Phase 2 before Phase 3 edge
findings.message: The edge is declared 'hard: journals must be born outside the repo, never migrated.' But the journal writes under ANCHOR_DATA_DIR via the existing paths.py seam — if it shipped before the move it would simply relocate with everything else through the same migrate_data pass Phase 2 already runs (append-only JSONL is the EASIEST store to migrate: no absolute paths inside, no rewrite map entries). The real cost of early birth is a week of journal files in git-status noise, solvable with one .gitignore line. Calling a preference a hard dependency matters because it's the stated reason C3 — 'the highest-value pillar' by the plan's own words — can't move earlier than fourth position. Either defend the edge with a real invariant (e.g. the parity gate's fixture paths) or downgrade it to 'preferred ordering' so a future re-cut isn't blocked by a phantom constraint.

The drain script parks PTY sessions (close_session + capture_session_docs) but says nothing about in-flight LANE JOBS, which until Phase 5 are children of the dashboard process and die with every nssm restart. The ritual runs at every wave across Phases 0–4 — on the order of 15+ restarts of the live service before restart survival exists. 'Never-broken increments' as John experiences it includes not silently killing a running Foreman build because a wave merged. The ritual needs one more line: check for active jobs (the lane locks / job dirs) and either wait for quiescence or get explicit go-ahead before restarting — otherwise the smoke ritual institutionalizes exactly the loss C4 exists to end.

The live gate derives views from 'a WRITE_LOCK-bracketed snapshot copy' — but WRITE_LOCK is the dashboard's in-process lock. Post-split, the supervisor appends to its segment and mutates job dirs outside that lock, so the snapshot is not consistent across processes: the gate can catch the supervisor between its emit and its legacy job-record write (tolerated as young journal-ahead) but ALSO between a job-dir write and the snapshot of the segment directory listing, producing spurious 'conflict' classifications that are ALWAYS BUG by decree. The plan built the writer model multi-process from day one but left the parity gate's quiescence mechanism single-process. State the cross-process snapshot rule (e.g. read segments AFTER legacy stores, so any skew presents as tolerated journal-ahead, never conflict) or the Phase-5 flip will manufacture flaky reds in the gate that must run 20-consecutive-green.

findings.section: The journal writer model — cli segment locking
findings.message: The cli segment's per-append lock is specified as msvcrt.locking — a Windows-only stdlib module. The inherited constraint (CLAUDE.md, enforced by distro.py's import scan) is that product code runs on any Python 3.8+ machine, with pywinpty the LONE platform exception, lazily imported in pty_manager only. journal.py importing msvcrt at module level creates a second platform-bound module and a distro-scan exception nobody approved. Specify the same idiom as the existing exception: lazy platform-guarded import with an fcntl.flock (or O_APPEND-atomicity) fallback on POSIX — the fix is one line in the plan now versus a distro-gate surprise in Phase 3.

The 20-consecutive-greens rule exists to catch time- and environment-dependent flakes before a walk joins the unattended 5AM run — quiescence races, overnight state, cold-start conditions. Explicitly allowing 20 accelerated back-to-back runs in one warm session 'to count' removes exactly the variance the gate samples for: a walk that flakes only against a cold service, a concurrent Foreman build, or the 5AM scheduled-task environment passes 20-in-a-row trivially. Steel-manned, the accelerated mode is fine as a FAST-FAIL filter but should not fully substitute: require some minimum of genuinely separated runs (e.g. ≥5 across distinct service restarts or nights) within the 20 before the walk is promoted.

The census classifies 'EVERY {…} interpolation in generate_html and render_project_window_html' — but those functions generate the ENTIRE page, including the server-rendered HTML body (task rows, project tiles, lane columns), which is interpolation-dense by design and NOT in C1's extraction scope (C1 names the JS/CSS blobs + the window shell). Read over the whole renderers, '>20 markup-emitting interpolations' is a near-certain trip — the amendment gate fires as a foregone conclusion, not a contingency. Read over only the extraction-scoped blobs, the threshold is plausible. The plan must pin the threshold's denominator to the extraction-scoped regions explicitly, or Phase 0 mechanically manufactures a spurious proposal-to-John amendment before Phase 1 ever starts.

A 'soak day' of warn-mode on a service with exactly one human user samples only the routes John happens to touch that day plus the healthcheck's walk. Rarely-used mutating routes (grass_export, move_project, term_delete, the .bat/.vbs launcher paths, scheduled tasks) may produce ZERO warn-log lines, and the gate then reads absence-of-warnings as safe-to-enforce — a false negative by construction. The Phase-0 consumer-enumeration inventory is the real evidence; the plan should say the enforce flip is gated on the INVENTORY having a verified token path per consumer, with the warn log demoted to a tripwire for consumers the inventory missed, not promoted as the primary gate artifact.

The path-audit tool scans DURABLE STORES (registry folder_path, worktree_path, discovery.json, job dirs) for absolute paths — but if the managed worktree base lives under ANCHOR_DATA_DIR and relocates, git itself holds absolute paths in a store the audit doesn't name: each main repo's .git/worktrees/<name>/gitdir and each worktree's .git file both point absolutely at each other. A rewrite of the registry's worktree_path without `git worktree repair` (or equivalent) leaves every parked/idle worktree — the ones W6 deliberately preserves across restarts — git-broken after the move, failing exactly the warm-resume path the boot-reaper dry-run is protecting. Add git worktree metadata to the audit's scan list and `git worktree repair` to the migration script, or state explicitly that the worktree base does not live under ANCHOR_DATA_DIR and therefore does not move.

Phase 0 bills the contract shim as its ONE behavior-bearing deploy, but the same phase also deploys the drain script into the live smoke ritual, injects sentinel comments via a pre-wave commit, and wires the ANCHOR_BUILD script tag into BOTH renderers (a change to the two most fragile functions in the codebase, pre-census, pre-freeze). The claim is rhetorically tidy but the renderers edit in particular deserves the same parity care Phase 1 formalizes — say that, rather than classifying it as non-behavior by fiat.

findings.section: Phase 4 — Declarative Route Table & Default-Deny Auth; Phase 1 ANCHOR_BOOT
findings.message: The plan never states which credential authenticates MUTATING requests from the browser after the cutover, and it explicitly defers CSRF hardening as 'Butler-era'. Walk it: Phase 1 declares window.ANCHOR_BOOT the ONLY server→client state channel and says it carries 'token presence' — not the token. So post-extraction, _postJson either (a) authenticates via the D3 cookie — an AMBIENT credential the browser attaches automatically, which is exactly the precondition for CSRF against localhost:8777 and the Tailscale-exposed PWA surface (a hostile page can fire authenticated POSTs to /api/rnd/term_input2, term_kill, move_project, push_now — i.e. keystroke injection into live agent terminals and destructive project ops), or (b) reads a token exposed to page JS, which is XSS-readable and contradicts the spirit of 'no URL tokens'. Nowhere does the plan specify SameSite, HttpOnly, Secure, or cookie scope. The header-token model being replaced was CSRF-immune by construction; D3's cookie model is not, so deferring CSRF is not a scope choice — it is shipping the auth pillar with a new vulnerability class the old model lacked. Phase 4 must specify: which credential POSTs use, SameSite=Strict (or Lax + origin check in the front-door hook), HttpOnly/Secure decisions, and a CSRF test in the gate. Until then C2's 'default-deny by construction' claim is refuted: the construction has an undesigned door.

findings.section: Phase 0 cookie spike / Phase 4 cookie application
findings.message: 'Cookie set at first tokened visit' is asserted but the FIRST tokened visit is never designed. A browser navigating to / sends no token; how does John's desktop browser, and especially the iPhone/iPad PWA over Tailscale HTTPS, deliver the token the first time on each client? If the answer is a one-time ?token= URL, that contradicts the North Star's 'no URL tokens except where WS demands it' unless the plan explicitly carves out a one-shot enrollment redirect that immediately sets the cookie and strips the URL (and states the history/log exposure of that one shot). If the answer is 'type it into a login form', that is a new page and a new open route that must appear in OPEN_ROUTES. The Phase-0 spike's acceptance questions cover cookie-through-WS-upgrade but not enrollment. This is a per-client design decision (desktop, PWA, Playwright fixtures, healthcheck walk) that gates the Phase-4 ops cutover — undesigned, it surfaces as a lockout during the cutover with John's daily tool on the line (C7 adjacency).

Phase 5 authenticates the supervisor's IPC 'with the same ANCHOR_TOKEN secret' that Phase 4 puts in browser cookies and retains in ?token= WS URLs (which land in browser history, proxy logs, and Tailscale Serve access logs). The supervisor is the process-spawning work plane — it launches claude.exe children under John's profile. Reusing the browser-exposed credential for it means any leak of the UI credential (XSS in the freshly-extracted 4,600-line JS blob, a logged WS URL, a shared screenshot) is immediately a spawn-capable credential. D2 says 'loopback token-authed IPC'; it does not mandate the SAME token. The plan should mint a separate supervisor IPC secret (delivered via AppEnvironmentExtra to both services, never to any client/browser), or explicitly record the shared-secret blast radius as an accepted risk with John's sign-off. One line of design now; a credential-tiering retrofit later.

findings.section: Phase 3 — idempotent event-replay tool + journal-first ordering
findings.message: Journal-first ordering plus emit() fail-open guarantees a class of journal-ahead events that represent mutations that NEVER committed to the authoritative store (crash or failure between emit and the legacy write). The plan then ships an 'idempotent event-replay tool: re-applying the journal against the legacy stores converges them' as 'the operational answer to a legacy-ahead or conflict classification'. Converging the authoritative store TOWARD the journal is a partial read-path-authority inversion — the exact thing D1 and the non-goal ('NOT promoting the event log to source of truth') forbid — and it can materialize records the system never made: an orphaned job_launch_requested or session-advance intent whose legacy write failed validation gets replayed into existence. The plan calls orphaned events 'benign intent records with an idempotent replay path' — benign only if replay distinguishes intent events from state-change events and refuses to fabricate from intents. Required: replay is operator-invoked, dry-run-first (stated), restores ONLY records the journal proves existed (state-change events with completed legacy correlates elsewhere), never auto-converges, and classifies orphaned intents as a separate non-replayable census line. Otherwise the recovery tool is the mechanism by which the 'lost from an index' fix becomes a 'fabricated into an index' bug.

findings.section: The journal writer model — seq/lock semantics
findings.message: The total order is defined as a global sort by (ts, writer_id, writer_seq). Wall-clock ts is not monotonic — an NTP step-back on PUTER makes writer_seq N+1 carry an EARLIER ts than N, and the global sort then reorders a single writer's own events, violating exactly the per-writer monotonic guarantee writer_seq exists to provide. Derived views are order-sensitive (session closed vs advanced, job launched vs cancelled), so a clock step during a live run silently derives wrong state and the parity gate reports phantom BUGs — or worse, matching-but-wrong views. The fix is cheap and should be stated in the writer model: a k-way merge that preserves each segment's writer_seq order absolutely (writer_seq dominates within a writer; ts only arbitrates ACROSS writers), plus a rule for cross-writer causality (causation_id ordering wins over ts when present). As written, the deterministic merge is deterministic but not correct.

The known highest-severity live weakness — the unauthenticated GET data plane serving /artifact, /project, /report (including domains/commercial.md-adjacent project data) — is scheduled fifth of seven phases, behind frontend extraction and hygiene, justified only by soak stability. The implicit compensating control (127.0.0.1 bind; Tailscale exposure gated on ANCHOR_TOKEN per the anchor-as-app research) is never stated in the plan. Either state it as the accepted interim control with an explicit 'no Tailscale Serve exposure of :8777 before the Phase-4 enforce flip' invariant asserted somewhere (healthcheck or checklist), or pull a coarse whole-plane token gate into Phase 0's shim deploy. Silence leaves the risk window unowned.

This host has ALREADY had the duplicate-supervisor incident (2026-06-08: rogue Anchor-Server NSSM service racing :8777 because the old code bound with SO_REUSEADDR). The plan's install script specifies ObjectName, env cloning, and NO_WINDOW discipline — but not the IPC port assignment, the 127.0.0.1-only bind, or the SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE single-instance guard the dashboard itself gained from that incident (paths.classify_bind_error/use_exclusive_bind exist and should be reused). A second service class with the same historical failure mode and none of the learned defenses is a regression waiting to recur. One sentence in Phase 5 fixes it.

findings.section: Phase 5 — IPC contract table + live probes
findings.message: Live probe (a) has the healthcheck 'ask the LIVE supervisor to spawn a trivial claude.exe --version child', implying the token-authed loopback API can be handed a command to run. If the IPC launch endpoint accepts arbitrary argv, the supervisor is an RCE-by-design endpoint gated by one shared secret (see the shared-token finding). The contract table should constrain the launch row to the guarded lane-launch path (the repo just landed 'relaunch goes through launch_guarded' — same principle), with the credentials/PATH probe as a dedicated, hardcoded probe endpoint that spawns a fixed binary, never a caller-supplied one.

The plan builds the allowlist MECHANISM (checked-in table, justification strings, live-match test) but never proposes the actual candidate open set — yet deciding which routes are open IS the security decision C2 exists to force. Likewise, C2 gates the data plane 'when ANCHOR_TOKEN is set'; the plan never states what default-deny means when the token is UNSET (everything open, as today? refuse to boot? warn banner?). Both belong in the plan as Phase-4 near-term specifics: a proposed candidate list (e.g. the 401 page itself, /vendor/brand favicon, the build-mismatch 409 path) and an explicit token-unset behavior asserted by the hybrid-state healthcheck check.

Whatever survives on the open allowlist remains reachable cross-origin via DNS rebinding despite the loopback bind (the browser resolves an attacker domain to 127.0.0.1 and same-origin policy no longer protects the responses; cookies won't be sent, but OPEN routes need none). A Host-header check (localhost/127.0.0.1/the Tailscale hostname) in the front-door hook is a few lines, covers every open route by construction, and closes the one attack that default-deny-with-allowlist structurally leaves open. Worth a bullet in the Phase-4 hook spec.

The ENFORCE-mode tripwire runs in the test suite; the distro-style scan covers only writes to journal/ paths. A production-only or hotfix code path that writes a legacy store WITHOUT going through a blessed wrapper is caught by neither — Tier-2 parity catches it eventually, but only for views the parity gate derives (session/effort), not for every store the census enumerated (rnd_jobs/ records, doc-persist commits). Close the triangle statically: extend the codebase-wide scan to forbid direct writes to the census-enumerated store paths from any module except the blessed wrappers, mirroring the journal.py rule. Otherwise C3's 'every mutation-of-record' claim rests on test coverage, not construction.

The warn log records who WOULD 401 and is reviewed as a gate artifact — it will therefore capture requests carrying ?token= query strings and cookie headers. State that the warn logger redacts credential values (token params, Cookie/Authorization headers) so the soak artifact isn't itself a credential store sitting in the repo or a gate attachment.

findings.section: The journal writer model — cli segment lock
findings.message: msvcrt.locking(LK_LOCK) retries for ~10 seconds then raises OSError rather than blocking indefinitely, and it locks a byte range relative to the current file position — under append the region to lock and the seek discipline need stating, and a contention-timeout needs a defined behavior (retry? fail-open into the emit-failure counter?). One sentence in the Phase-3 journal.py spec prevents an implementer from discovering these semantics mid-wave.

reviews.note: Skeptic Shark pass, future-maintainer angle. The revision is substantially stronger, but the writer model and the flag/revertibility story contain internal contradictions a maintainer will hit in year one.

findings.topic: static-vs-embedded off-switch flag contradicts C1 blob deletion
findings.section: DAG intro (revertibility claim) · Phase 1 exit gate · Phase 6 deferred list
findings.message: The plan claims globally that 'each merged wave is revertible without reverting later waves via the four per-pillar off-switch flags', and Phase 6 explicitly DEFERS removing all four flags ('they stay as supported operational levers until the Butler effort decides otherwise'). But a functional static-vs-embedded flag requires the embedded blob to still exist — and C1's Phase-1 exit gate requires the blob GONE (net ≥7,000-line shrink measured at the phase-end commit, 'no embedded frontend blob larger than ~50 lines'). You cannot simultaneously delete 7,300 lines from anchor_gui.py and keep a runtime lever that re-serves them. As written, a future maintainer reading the hybrid-state matrix will find a named, 'supported' configuration (embedded frontend) that has no code behind it — or worse, the team will keep the blob alive in some retrievable form to honor the matrix, silently failing C1. Pick one: the flag dies at Phase-1 exit (revert = git revert, stated honestly, and the DAG's revertibility claim is corrected to three flags), or the C1 bar is amended. The plan currently asserts both.

findings.topic: ts-first merge key defeats per-writer seq and causal order
findings.message: The total order is 'sort by (ts, writer_id, writer_seq)'. Because ts is the PRIMARY key, a backward wall-clock step (NTP correction, DST-adjacent skew) reorders a SINGLE writer's own events against its own monotonic writer_seq — the exact property writer_seq exists to guarantee. Cross-writer it is worse: the dashboard's job_launch_requested and the supervisor's job_launched are causally ordered but their wall clocks are independent; a few-ms inversion puts the result before the intent in every derivation, parity run, and rebuild_index replay. The envelope carries correlation_id and causation_id, yet the merge ignores both. Deterministic ≠ correct: the parity gate will re-derive views in a causally wrong order and either flag phantom divergence or, worse, converge on a wrong-but-stable derivation a future maintainer cannot debug. Fix: within a writer, writer_seq must dominate (merge segments as already-ordered streams, k-way merged by ts only ACROSS writers), and cross-writer causal pairs need causation_id-aware ordering or an explicit tolerance rule in the parity gate.

findings.topic: orphaned intent events become permanent false BUGs
findings.section: Journal writer model / Phase 3 two-tier parity gate / Phase 5 emitter handover
findings.message: Post-split, the dashboard emits job_launch_requested, then IPCs the supervisor, which emits job_launched. If the IPC hop or the launch itself fails, the intent event is journaled but no legacy job record ever exists — a journal-ahead event that ages past the tail window and is then, by the plan's own rule, 'classified BUG'. Every legitimately failed launch attempt therefore becomes a permanent parity-gate BUG. The ownership table's job family (launched/finished/cancelled/gate_asked/gate_answered) contains no job_launch_failed or intent-expired compensating event, and the parity rules have no notion of an intent whose correlation chain legitimately terminated without a store write. A gate that cries BUG on a normal failure path trains the future maintainer to ignore BUG — killing the one signal C3 exists to provide. The plan needs either a compensating failure event owned per the table, or an explicit parity rule for intent-kind events with terminated correlation chains.

findings.topic: per-TYPE ownership table is the wrong granularity under inline mode
findings.section: Journal writer model — emitter-ownership table / failure mode (b)
findings.message: The invariant is 'exactly ONE owning writer per event type, checked in' — but mode:'inline' makes ownership follow the JOB HANDLE, which is per-job, not per-type. During a supervisor flap (dashboard's IPC times out and falls back inline while the supervisor is actually alive, or the supervisor recovers mid-degradation), job_finished events for different jobs legitimately appear in BOTH segments in the same window — and a false-degradation race can produce the same job launched twice (once inline, once supervised) under one correlation_id. The tripwire, parity gate, and payload-completeness gate 'all read the same table', but a static per-type table cannot adjudicate which writer was legitimate for which event at which instant. As specified, the gates either accept any writer for the job family (the invariant is unenforceable theater) or flag legitimate inline emissions as violations. The table needs a per-event legitimacy rule (e.g., ownership resolved by which process's job dir holds the handle record, checkable at verification time) and the degraded-mode transition needs a walked scenario like the C4 one — it is currently the least-specified failure mode in a section that prides itself on enumerating six.

findings.topic: cookie bootstrap flow never specified
findings.section: Phase 4 — cookie verdict application / ops-cutover gate
findings.message: C2 requires 'browser page navigation still working (cookie or equivalent)'. The plan spikes cookie-THROUGH-WS survival and applies the verdict in Phase 4, and the ops-cutover gate mints a token into NSSM env — but nowhere does any phase specify how John's browser ACQUIRES the cookie in the first place: no login/handshake route, no Set-Cookie flow, no OPEN_ROUTES entry for a bootstrap path, no statement of cookie attributes (HttpOnly, SameSite, lifetime) or re-establishment after expiry on the iPad PWA over Tailscale. The day the tokenless-401 live assert passes, GET / itself is gated — with what, exactly, in the browser? A future maintainer (or John at 7am) hits a 401 on the home page with no documented way in. This is the single most user-visible seam in the whole auth pillar and it is the one left implicit. The cookie-establishment flow must be a named Phase-4 deliverable with its own OPEN_ROUTES-reviewed entry.

findings.topic: shrink measurement definition internally inconsistent
findings.section: Phase 1 — shrink measurement / census margin arithmetic
findings.message: 'The NET wc -l delta on anchor_gui.py … with ALL new seam code counted against it wherever it lives' is self-contradictory: a single-file wc -l delta on anchor_gui.py mechanically CANNOT count seam code that lives in other files (bootstrap builder module, static-route wiring elsewhere). The census arithmetic (gross − ≤400 seam) reveals the intent, but the formal gate definition a Foreman wave will actually execute is ambiguous — is the number delta(anchor_gui.py), or delta(anchor_gui.py) minus new lines added in named seam files? Two readings differ by up to the whole seam budget, i.e., potentially the entire stated margin. State the formula explicitly: net = (pre-tag wc − phase-end wc on anchor_gui.py) − Σ(new lines in an enumerated seam-file list).

findings.topic: msvcrt lock is Windows-only in a cross-platform module
findings.section: Journal writer model — cli segment lock / Phase 3 journal.py
findings.message: journal.py takes an msvcrt.locking per-append lock on the cli segment. msvcrt is Windows-only; the repo's binding constraint (enforced by distro.py's import scan philosophy) is 'must run on any machine with Python 3.8+', with ONLY pywinpty exempted and ONLY behind a lazy terminal-only import. journal.py is core shared code imported by the dashboard, the supervisor, and anchor.py — an unconditional msvcrt import breaks every non-Windows consumer of anchor.py, and even a lazy import leaves the CLI-writer path undefined off-Windows. Name the portable strategy (fcntl/msvcrt shim, or O_APPEND single-write-per-line semantics which are atomic enough for short lines on both platforms) or declare and justify a second platform exception through the same reviewed path pywinpty got.

findings.topic: healthcheck process is an unmodeled fourth writer
findings.message: The writer set is closed at dashboard/supervisor/cli, yet the envelope's actor.kind already anticipates 'healthcheck-synthetic' — and anchor_healthcheck.py is a FOURTH OS process that boots an in-process server and exercises mutating endpoints. Its v2–v5 walks use temp ANCHOR_DATA_DIRs (journals go to temp — fine), but the plan never PROVES that every healthcheck mutation is temp-scoped once the tripwire's ENFORCE mode and the journal instrumentation are live; any journaled mutation it performs against the real data dir would append to the 'dashboard' segment from a second process, violating single-writer-per-file — the model's foundational invariant — silently. Either give the healthcheck process its own writer_id/segment, or add an explicit gate asserting the healthcheck emits zero events into the live journal directory. The reviser caught the CLI's third-writer hole; this is the same hole one process over.

findings.topic: supervisor's real journal emission never asserted live
findings.message: The claim 'the C3 completeness guarantee survives the split with zero exceptions' rests entirely on the inline seam and the stub-seam matrix — both exercise the IN-PROCESS emit path. The two live probes (spawn claude.exe --version; restart supervisor with sacrificial child) assert credentials and job-object breakaway but never assert that the REAL supervisor service, under its NSSM account with its AppEnvironmentExtra-cloned env, actually wrote job events to its own segment with correct writer_seq recovery. Env drift (ANCHOR_DATA_DIR missing from the cloned env, path resolution under the service account) is exactly the failure class inline tests cannot see. Add one line to probe (a) or the C4 runbook: after the live job, assert its lifecycle events are present in the supervisor segment on disk. Cheap, and it closes the only untested writer.

findings.topic: Phase 0 undersized at M for thirteen deliverables
findings.message: Phase 0 is sized M (2–3 Foreman waves) yet enumerates ~13 deliverables including a census SCRIPT, five scripted Playwright stateful flows (terminal-open-and-type via stub PTY is not an afternoon), a full consumer inventory across launchers/scheduled tasks/personal scripts, the tripwire wrapper run across suite+healthcheck, a shipped-and-live-deployed contract shim touching both renderers plus _postJson plus a server-side 409 path, a shipped drain script, sentinel anchors + a freshness gate, TWO time-boxed spikes with real-client testing (iPhone PWA over Tailscale), healthcheck_repeat.py, and three process codifications. That is 4–5 waves of work labeled as 2–3. A future maintainer inheriting the plan mid-effort reads the sizing as commitments; an undersized foundation phase is how 'never-broken increments' gets rushed. Re-size honestly or explicitly move the Playwright flows and healthcheck_repeat.py into the trailing-allowed set alongside the spikes.

findings.topic: Phase 4 wall-clock serialization unaccounted
findings.section: Phase 4 — warn-mode soak / zero-arms exit gate
findings.message: Each route batch requires: deploy warn → soak A DAY on the live service → review warn log as a gate artifact → deploy enforce, and auth flips may never share a deploy with the JS that calls them. With ~125 arms in 'small reviewed batches', that is weeks of serialized wall clock — none of which is captured by 'L (3–4 waves)', and all of which now sits behind a BLOCKING exit gate (zero arms). The predictable failure mode is batch inflation near phase end to close the gate — exactly the rushed migration the soak discipline exists to prevent. State the batch size and expected batch count, or explicitly allow warn-soaks for multiple batches to overlap, so the exit gate's cost is sized rather than discovered.

findings.topic: old-data-dir read-only week vs Phase 6 conclusion timing
findings.message: Phase 2 preserves the old data dir 'read-only for a week'; Phase 6 — several L phases later — 'concludes the old data dir's read-only week'. Those are months apart. Either the retention is actually until-Phase-6 (say so) or the week concludes inside Phase 2/3 and Phase 6's line is dead text.

findings.topic: shim injection undermines the 'pure verbatim move' claim
findings.message: Phase 0 injects the ANCHOR_BUILD script tag into BOTH renderers and X-Anchor-Build into _postJson; Phase 1 then calls increment 1 a 'pure verbatim move, census-confirmed zero interpolations' and separately 'absorbs' the build id into ANCHOR_BOOT. The moved blob is post-shim, and the absorption is a real edit during the move — so the pinned-fixture diff will carry shim deltas that must appear on the enumerated-delta token list. Not a design flaw, but the 'pure verbatim / zero interpolations' language will be false by a few lines the moment Phase 0 ships; pre-list the shim tokens now so the first parity run doesn't open with a gate failure.

reviews.note: Contrarian pass, steel-man-the-premise angle: the plan's structure is strong, so I pressed on its load-bearing premises — the sequencing rationale, the writer-model's ordering guarantees, the parity-gate semantics, and the unexamined interactions with existing safety machinery.

findings.topic: supervisor split vs zombie-hunter live-owner semantics
findings.message: The plan moves job ownership into a separate process but never mentions the armed orphan-kill machinery that keys off in-process job state. Today's orphan discriminator (zombie_hunter.live_owner_ids) computes 'live owner' from the DASHBOARD'S view: PTY-attached set ∪ job_runner._holder_is_active ∪ parent-owned. Post-split, the dashboard no longer holds the job handles — _holder_is_active in the dashboard process will report supervisor-owned jobs as NOT active, so a supervisor-owned session with no open browser stream becomes classifiable as an orphan and the Swarm View / armed kill-daemon can freeze or kill exactly the work the split exists to protect. The repo marks this discriminator SAFETY-CRITICAL (2026-06-30). The in-memory rebuild table covers dashboard structures (_LIVE, _JOB_DIRS, lane locks) but zombie-hunter's live-owner provider is not a rebuild row and is not named anywhere in Phase 5. The C4 live demo could pass (short window, daemon not firing) while the regression ships. Phase 5 needs an explicit row: live_owner_ids' job_active provider must query the supervisor (or the merged journal) before the external seam goes live.

findings.topic: Phase 5 gated behind zero-legacy-arms unnecessarily
findings.section: Dependency DAG & sequencing rationale / Phase 4 exit gate
findings.message: The DAG edge 'Phase 5 after Phase 4' is justified by IPC reusing the route-table module + token helper — but that module exists on DAY ONE of Phase 4 (rows-first: every route gets a declared row immediately). What the plan actually gates Phase 5 behind is Phase 4's new C2-BLOCKING exit gate: migrating ~125 handler bodies to zero legacy arms across 3–4 waves. The supervisor consumes none of that handler migration. Meanwhile C4 — the restart-survival keystone the North Star calls non-negotiable, and the one pillar relieving John's real daily pain (every restart kills in-flight jobs) — lands last among pillars, behind weeks of mechanical body migration, and every per-wave smoke ritual in Phases 0–4 performs an nssm restart that kills any in-flight job. Steel-manning the plan's own 'highest-value first' re-cut logic (used to pull the journal forward), the same logic says Phase 5's jobs-half can start once the table module + warn-mode auth + the Phase-3 ownership table exist, concurrent with or immediately after the enforce flips — not after the zero-arms drive-down. The hard gate is right for C2; making it a prerequisite for C4 is an over-constrained edge the DAG should either relax or explicitly defend.

findings.topic: journal-ahead: benign-intent vs BUG contradiction
findings.section: Phase 3 — journal-first write order / two-tier parity gate
findings.message: Two commitments contradict. Journal-first-by-decree says an orphaned journal event (emit succeeded, legacy write then failed or the process crashed between them) is 'a benign intent record with an idempotent replay path.' The Tier-2 gate says journal-ahead OLDER than the tail window 'is classified BUG.' The crash-between-writes case — the exact scenario journal-first is designed to make benign — produces precisely a beyond-window journal-ahead event, so the designed-for, called-benign failure mode is permanently flagged BUG by the gate that proves C3. Either the classification needs a reconciled/acknowledged state (journal-ahead + replay-tool-converged → resolved, not BUG), or 'benign' is the wrong word and the plan should say every orphan is a defect requiring operator replay. As written, the first real crash makes the daily parity gate red forever with no defined path back to green, which corrodes the gate's authority (C7's 'suite stays green' meets a gate that can't self-heal).

findings.topic: wall-clock merge order not causally safe
findings.section: The journal writer model — seq/lock semantics
findings.message: The total order for derivation, parity, and replay is sort-by (ts, writer_id, writer_seq). Wall clocks — even on one machine — step backwards (NTP correction, resume-from-sleep on a desktop that sleeps nightly), and ts resolution ties across writers are resolved LEXICALLY, which happens to sort 'dashboard' before 'supervisor' today but is a coincidence, not a design. A causally-ordered pair (dashboard job_launch_requested → supervisor job_launched → supervisor job_finished) can merge out of order under a clock step, and rebuild_index / the replay tool — whose correctness IS criterion C3's 'provably derivable' — silently apply last-write-wins reductions in the wrong order. The envelope already carries causation_id; the merge should use it (or a hybrid logical clock: max(seen_ts+1, wall)) as a tie-and-regression breaker, and the parity gate should classify a causation edge that sorts backwards as BUG. Right now clock regression is the one failure mode NOT in the enumerated six, and it's the one that corrupts derivation rather than just losing a line.

findings.topic: contract shim missing-header policy unspecified
findings.message: The shim's protection premise has a hole at both ends. (1) Clients that predate the shim deploy — the already-open stale tab and the PWA-cached iPad client, the two named beneficiaries — never send X-Anchor-Build at all, and the plan doesn't say what the server does with a MISSING header. Reject it and you break anchor_healthcheck.py's endpoint walk, the CLI, and every personal script (a C7 breakage in the 'one behavior-bearing deploy'); allow it and every pre-shim client silently bypasses the shim, so the mechanism only protects tabs opened AFTER the deploy that needed protecting least. (2) The carrier rides _postJson only — WS/SSE attach and GET navigations from a stale client carry no build id, so a stale tab can hold a live terminal WebSocket across a protocol-changing deploy unchecked. The shim needs a stated missing-header policy (allow + log, with the banner delivered by a different channel for pre-shim clients, e.g. a version probe on next poll) and an honest statement of which surfaces it does NOT cover.

findings.topic: data-dir-before-journal 'hard dependency' is actually soft
findings.section: Dependency DAG — Phase 2 before Phase 3 edge
findings.message: The edge is declared 'hard: journals must be born outside the repo, never migrated.' But the journal writes under ANCHOR_DATA_DIR via the existing paths.py seam — if it shipped before the move it would simply relocate with everything else through the same migrate_data pass Phase 2 already runs (append-only JSONL is the EASIEST store to migrate: no absolute paths inside, no rewrite map entries). The real cost of early birth is a week of journal files in git-status noise, solvable with one .gitignore line. Calling a preference a hard dependency matters because it's the stated reason C3 — 'the highest-value pillar' by the plan's own words — can't move earlier than fourth position. Either defend the edge with a real invariant (e.g. the parity gate's fixture paths) or downgrade it to 'preferred ordering' so a future re-cut isn't blocked by a phantom constraint.

findings.topic: per-wave smoke restarts kill in-flight jobs pre-split
findings.message: The drain script parks PTY sessions (close_session + capture_session_docs) but says nothing about in-flight LANE JOBS, which until Phase 5 are children of the dashboard process and die with every nssm restart. The ritual runs at every wave across Phases 0–4 — on the order of 15+ restarts of the live service before restart survival exists. 'Never-broken increments' as John experiences it includes not silently killing a running Foreman build because a wave merged. The ritual needs one more line: check for active jobs (the lane locks / job dirs) and either wait for quiescence or get explicit go-ahead before restarting — otherwise the smoke ritual institutionalizes exactly the loss C4 exists to end.

findings.topic: Tier-2 snapshot quiescence is single-process
findings.message: The live gate derives views from 'a WRITE_LOCK-bracketed snapshot copy' — but WRITE_LOCK is the dashboard's in-process lock. Post-split, the supervisor appends to its segment and mutates job dirs outside that lock, so the snapshot is not consistent across processes: the gate can catch the supervisor between its emit and its legacy job-record write (tolerated as young journal-ahead) but ALSO between a job-dir write and the snapshot of the segment directory listing, producing spurious 'conflict' classifications that are ALWAYS BUG by decree. The plan built the writer model multi-process from day one but left the parity gate's quiescence mechanism single-process. State the cross-process snapshot rule (e.g. read segments AFTER legacy stores, so any skew presents as tolerated journal-ahead, never conflict) or the Phase-5 flip will manufacture flaky reds in the gate that must run 20-consecutive-green.

findings.topic: msvcrt lock breaks cross-platform constraint
findings.section: The journal writer model — cli segment locking
findings.message: The cli segment's per-append lock is specified as msvcrt.locking — a Windows-only stdlib module. The inherited constraint (CLAUDE.md, enforced by distro.py's import scan) is that product code runs on any Python 3.8+ machine, with pywinpty the LONE platform exception, lazily imported in pty_manager only. journal.py importing msvcrt at module level creates a second platform-bound module and a distro-scan exception nobody approved. Specify the same idiom as the existing exception: lazy platform-guarded import with an fcntl.flock (or O_APPEND-atomicity) fallback on POSIX — the fix is one line in the plan now versus a distro-gate surprise in Phase 3.

findings.topic: accelerated 20-greens guts the flake gate's premise
findings.message: The 20-consecutive-greens rule exists to catch time- and environment-dependent flakes before a walk joins the unattended 5AM run — quiescence races, overnight state, cold-start conditions. Explicitly allowing 20 accelerated back-to-back runs in one warm session 'to count' removes exactly the variance the gate samples for: a walk that flakes only against a cold service, a concurrent Foreman build, or the 5AM scheduled-task environment passes 20-in-a-row trivially. Steel-manned, the accelerated mode is fine as a FAST-FAIL filter but should not fully substitute: require some minimum of genuinely separated runs (e.g. ≥5 across distinct service restarts or nights) within the 20 before the walk is promoted.

findings.topic: interpolation-census scope vs the >20 threshold is ambiguous
findings.message: The census classifies 'EVERY {…} interpolation in generate_html and render_project_window_html' — but those functions generate the ENTIRE page, including the server-rendered HTML body (task rows, project tiles, lane columns), which is interpolation-dense by design and NOT in C1's extraction scope (C1 names the JS/CSS blobs + the window shell). Read over the whole renderers, '>20 markup-emitting interpolations' is a near-certain trip — the amendment gate fires as a foregone conclusion, not a contingency. Read over only the extraction-scoped blobs, the threshold is plausible. The plan must pin the threshold's denominator to the extraction-scoped regions explicitly, or Phase 0 mechanically manufactures a spurious proposal-to-John amendment before Phase 1 ever starts.

findings.topic: warn-mode soak coverage on a single-user service
findings.message: A 'soak day' of warn-mode on a service with exactly one human user samples only the routes John happens to touch that day plus the healthcheck's walk. Rarely-used mutating routes (grass_export, move_project, term_delete, the .bat/.vbs launcher paths, scheduled tasks) may produce ZERO warn-log lines, and the gate then reads absence-of-warnings as safe-to-enforce — a false negative by construction. The Phase-0 consumer-enumeration inventory is the real evidence; the plan should say the enforce flip is gated on the INVENTORY having a verified token path per consumer, with the warn log demoted to a tripwire for consumers the inventory missed, not promoted as the primary gate artifact.

findings.topic: path-audit misses git's own worktree metadata
findings.message: The path-audit tool scans DURABLE STORES (registry folder_path, worktree_path, discovery.json, job dirs) for absolute paths — but if the managed worktree base lives under ANCHOR_DATA_DIR and relocates, git itself holds absolute paths in a store the audit doesn't name: each main repo's .git/worktrees/<name>/gitdir and each worktree's .git file both point absolutely at each other. A rewrite of the registry's worktree_path without `git worktree repair` (or equivalent) leaves every parked/idle worktree — the ones W6 deliberately preserves across restarts — git-broken after the move, failing exactly the warm-resume path the boot-reaper dry-run is protecting. Add git worktree metadata to the audit's scan list and `git worktree repair` to the migration script, or state explicitly that the worktree base does not live under ANCHOR_DATA_DIR and therefore does not move.

findings.topic: 'ONE behavior-bearing deploy' claim is overstated
findings.message: Phase 0 bills the contract shim as its ONE behavior-bearing deploy, but the same phase also deploys the drain script into the live smoke ritual, injects sentinel comments via a pre-wave commit, and wires the ANCHOR_BUILD script tag into BOTH renderers (a change to the two most fragile functions in the codebase, pre-census, pre-freeze). The claim is rhetorically tidy but the renderers edit in particular deserves the same parity care Phase 1 formalizes — say that, rather than classifying it as non-behavior by fiat.

reviews.note: Analyst Shark, pressed through the security angle. The plan's auth pillar (C2) has real structural gaps around the cookie mechanism it locked in D3; the journal (C3) has two integrity defects; the supervisor (C4) has blast-radius and single-instance gaps the repo's own incident history warns about.

findings.topic: cookie auth CSRF posture undefined
findings.section: Phase 4 — Declarative Route Table & Default-Deny Auth; Phase 1 ANCHOR_BOOT
findings.message: The plan never states which credential authenticates MUTATING requests from the browser after the cutover, and it explicitly defers CSRF hardening as 'Butler-era'. Walk it: Phase 1 declares window.ANCHOR_BOOT the ONLY server→client state channel and says it carries 'token presence' — not the token. So post-extraction, _postJson either (a) authenticates via the D3 cookie — an AMBIENT credential the browser attaches automatically, which is exactly the precondition for CSRF against localhost:8777 and the Tailscale-exposed PWA surface (a hostile page can fire authenticated POSTs to /api/rnd/term_input2, term_kill, move_project, push_now — i.e. keystroke injection into live agent terminals and destructive project ops), or (b) reads a token exposed to page JS, which is XSS-readable and contradicts the spirit of 'no URL tokens'. Nowhere does the plan specify SameSite, HttpOnly, Secure, or cookie scope. The header-token model being replaced was CSRF-immune by construction; D3's cookie model is not, so deferring CSRF is not a scope choice — it is shipping the auth pillar with a new vulnerability class the old model lacked. Phase 4 must specify: which credential POSTs use, SameSite=Strict (or Lax + origin check in the front-door hook), HttpOnly/Secure decisions, and a CSRF test in the gate. Until then C2's 'default-deny by construction' claim is refuted: the construction has an undesigned door.

findings.topic: cookie bootstrap/enrollment flow unspecified
findings.section: Phase 0 cookie spike / Phase 4 cookie application
findings.message: 'Cookie set at first tokened visit' is asserted but the FIRST tokened visit is never designed. A browser navigating to / sends no token; how does John's desktop browser, and especially the iPhone/iPad PWA over Tailscale HTTPS, deliver the token the first time on each client? If the answer is a one-time ?token= URL, that contradicts the North Star's 'no URL tokens except where WS demands it' unless the plan explicitly carves out a one-shot enrollment redirect that immediately sets the cookie and strips the URL (and states the history/log exposure of that one shot). If the answer is 'type it into a login form', that is a new page and a new open route that must appear in OPEN_ROUTES. The Phase-0 spike's acceptance questions cover cookie-through-WS-upgrade but not enrollment. This is a per-client design decision (desktop, PWA, Playwright fixtures, healthcheck walk) that gates the Phase-4 ops cutover — undesigned, it surfaces as a lockout during the cutover with John's daily tool on the line (C7 adjacency).

findings.topic: single shared token across control and work planes
findings.message: Phase 5 authenticates the supervisor's IPC 'with the same ANCHOR_TOKEN secret' that Phase 4 puts in browser cookies and retains in ?token= WS URLs (which land in browser history, proxy logs, and Tailscale Serve access logs). The supervisor is the process-spawning work plane — it launches claude.exe children under John's profile. Reusing the browser-exposed credential for it means any leak of the UI credential (XSS in the freshly-extracted 4,600-line JS blob, a logged WS URL, a shared screenshot) is immediately a spawn-capable credential. D2 says 'loopback token-authed IPC'; it does not mandate the SAME token. The plan should mint a separate supervisor IPC secret (delivered via AppEnvironmentExtra to both services, never to any client/browser), or explicitly record the shared-secret blast radius as an accepted risk with John's sign-off. One line of design now; a credential-tiering retrofit later.

findings.topic: replay tool inverts dual-write authority
findings.section: Phase 3 — idempotent event-replay tool + journal-first ordering
findings.message: Journal-first ordering plus emit() fail-open guarantees a class of journal-ahead events that represent mutations that NEVER committed to the authoritative store (crash or failure between emit and the legacy write). The plan then ships an 'idempotent event-replay tool: re-applying the journal against the legacy stores converges them' as 'the operational answer to a legacy-ahead or conflict classification'. Converging the authoritative store TOWARD the journal is a partial read-path-authority inversion — the exact thing D1 and the non-goal ('NOT promoting the event log to source of truth') forbid — and it can materialize records the system never made: an orphaned job_launch_requested or session-advance intent whose legacy write failed validation gets replayed into existence. The plan calls orphaned events 'benign intent records with an idempotent replay path' — benign only if replay distinguishes intent events from state-change events and refuses to fabricate from intents. Required: replay is operator-invoked, dry-run-first (stated), restores ONLY records the journal proves existed (state-change events with completed legacy correlates elsewhere), never auto-converges, and classifies orphaned intents as a separate non-replayable census line. Otherwise the recovery tool is the mechanism by which the 'lost from an index' fix becomes a 'fabricated into an index' bug.

findings.topic: merge order violates per-writer ordering under clock regression
findings.section: The journal writer model — seq/lock semantics
findings.message: The total order is defined as a global sort by (ts, writer_id, writer_seq). Wall-clock ts is not monotonic — an NTP step-back on PUTER makes writer_seq N+1 carry an EARLIER ts than N, and the global sort then reorders a single writer's own events, violating exactly the per-writer monotonic guarantee writer_seq exists to provide. Derived views are order-sensitive (session closed vs advanced, job launched vs cancelled), so a clock step during a live run silently derives wrong state and the parity gate reports phantom BUGs — or worse, matching-but-wrong views. The fix is cheap and should be stated in the writer model: a k-way merge that preserves each segment's writer_seq order absolutely (writer_seq dominates within a writer; ts only arbitrates ACROSS writers), plus a rule for cross-writer causality (causation_id ordering wins over ts when present). As written, the deterministic merge is deterministic but not correct.

findings.topic: open GET plane persists until Phase 4 with compensating control unstated
findings.message: The known highest-severity live weakness — the unauthenticated GET data plane serving /artifact, /project, /report (including domains/commercial.md-adjacent project data) — is scheduled fifth of seven phases, behind frontend extraction and hygiene, justified only by soak stability. The implicit compensating control (127.0.0.1 bind; Tailscale exposure gated on ANCHOR_TOKEN per the anchor-as-app research) is never stated in the plan. Either state it as the accepted interim control with an explicit 'no Tailscale Serve exposure of :8777 before the Phase-4 enforce flip' invariant asserted somewhere (healthcheck or checklist), or pull a coarse whole-plane token gate into Phase 0's shim deploy. Silence leaves the risk window unowned.

findings.topic: supervisor port/bind/single-instance guard unspecified
findings.message: This host has ALREADY had the duplicate-supervisor incident (2026-06-08: rogue Anchor-Server NSSM service racing :8777 because the old code bound with SO_REUSEADDR). The plan's install script specifies ObjectName, env cloning, and NO_WINDOW discipline — but not the IPC port assignment, the 127.0.0.1-only bind, or the SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE single-instance guard the dashboard itself gained from that incident (paths.classify_bind_error/use_exclusive_bind exist and should be reused). A second service class with the same historical failure mode and none of the learned defenses is a regression waiting to recur. One sentence in Phase 5 fixes it.

findings.topic: IPC spawn surface unconstrained
findings.section: Phase 5 — IPC contract table + live probes
findings.message: Live probe (a) has the healthcheck 'ask the LIVE supervisor to spawn a trivial claude.exe --version child', implying the token-authed loopback API can be handed a command to run. If the IPC launch endpoint accepts arbitrary argv, the supervisor is an RCE-by-design endpoint gated by one shared secret (see the shared-token finding). The contract table should constrain the launch row to the guarded lane-launch path (the repo just landed 'relaunch goes through launch_guarded' — same principle), with the credentials/PATH probe as a dedicated, hardcoded probe endpoint that spawns a fixed binary, never a caller-supplied one.

findings.topic: OPEN_ROUTES candidates and token-unset semantics absent
findings.message: The plan builds the allowlist MECHANISM (checked-in table, justification strings, live-match test) but never proposes the actual candidate open set — yet deciding which routes are open IS the security decision C2 exists to force. Likewise, C2 gates the data plane 'when ANCHOR_TOKEN is set'; the plan never states what default-deny means when the token is UNSET (everything open, as today? refuse to boot? warn banner?). Both belong in the plan as Phase-4 near-term specifics: a proposed candidate list (e.g. the 401 page itself, /vendor/brand favicon, the build-mismatch 409 path) and an explicit token-unset behavior asserted by the hybrid-state healthcheck check.

findings.topic: no Host-header validation for open routes
findings.message: Whatever survives on the open allowlist remains reachable cross-origin via DNS rebinding despite the loopback bind (the browser resolves an attacker domain to 127.0.0.1 and same-origin policy no longer protects the responses; cookies won't be sent, but OPEN routes need none). A Host-header check (localhost/127.0.0.1/the Tailscale hostname) in the front-door hook is a few lines, covers every open route by construction, and closes the one attack that default-deny-with-allowlist structurally leaves open. Worth a bullet in the Phase-4 hook spec.

findings.topic: tripwire enforcement is tests-only
findings.message: The ENFORCE-mode tripwire runs in the test suite; the distro-style scan covers only writes to journal/ paths. A production-only or hotfix code path that writes a legacy store WITHOUT going through a blessed wrapper is caught by neither — Tier-2 parity catches it eventually, but only for views the parity gate derives (session/effort), not for every store the census enumerated (rnd_jobs/ records, doc-persist commits). Close the triangle statically: extend the codebase-wide scan to forbid direct writes to the census-enumerated store paths from any module except the blessed wrappers, mirroring the journal.py rule. Otherwise C3's 'every mutation-of-record' claim rests on test coverage, not construction.

findings.topic: warn-mode log hygiene
findings.message: The warn log records who WOULD 401 and is reviewed as a gate artifact — it will therefore capture requests carrying ?token= query strings and cookie headers. State that the warn logger redacts credential values (token params, Cookie/Authorization headers) so the soak artifact isn't itself a credential store sitting in the repo or a gate attachment.

findings.topic: msvcrt.locking semantics on the cli segment
findings.section: The journal writer model — cli segment lock
findings.message: msvcrt.locking(LK_LOCK) retries for ~10 seconds then raises OSError rather than blocking indefinitely, and it locks a byte range relative to the current file position — under append the region to lock and the seek discipline need stating, and a contention-timeout needs a defined behavior (retry? fail-open into the emit-failure counter?). One sentence in the Phase-3 journal.py spec prevents an implementer from discovering these semantics mid-wave.
